```ts
const base = slot * 8; // per slot: px, py, pz, qx, qy, qz, qw, flags
const pos = [views.curr[base], views.curr[base + 1], views.curr[base + 2]];
const vel = handle.world.linearVelocity(ball) ? [views.scratch[12], views.scratch[13], views.scratch[14]] : null;
console.log(pos, vel, handle.world.stateHash(), handle.world.tick());
handle.world.free();
```

| Gotcha | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| `SimEntry` | `{ sceneId: string; desc: EntityDescJson }`. `sceneId` is the scene `id` (or `__ground`, `__bounds.minX`...); `desc` is what `World.spawn` parses. Spawning `x.sim` in order gives the same ids and the same `stateHash` as `createGame` (for scenes without auto-hull glTF entities; `createGame` spawns those last, see `game.ts`). |
| `environment.ground` is spawned too | It is the first entry (`__ground`): a static infinite half-space at `ground.y` with friction 0.5, restitution 0; `size` only sizes the visible plane. So Node and the browser share the floor; you do not need a box entity for it. |
| `pendingHulls` | glTF entities with an auto convex hull have empty `points` until the renderer reads the mesh. Node has no renderer: skip them (above), or give those entities an explicit primitive collider. |
| `StateViews(handle)` | Takes a `SimHandle` (only `world` and `memory` are read). Views are byte-offset windows on `memory.buffer`; they go stale when wasm memory grows or the world's buffers grow (spawning), which is what `refresh()` checks. Never keep a raw `Float32Array` across a spawn. |
| Velocity and queries | `linearVelocity`, `angularVelocity`, `characterState`, `raycast` write into `views.scratch` and return `false` when there is nothing to write (offsets in [api-reference.md](../api-reference.md#scratch-buffer)). Read the scratch right away; the next query overwrites it. |
| Allocating reads | `world.transformOf(id)` returns a fresh `Float32Array` (`[px, py, pz, qx, qy, qz, qw]`) or undefined: fine in a test, not in a per-tick path. |
| More worlds | `const World = handle.world.constructor as new (seed: number, g: number) => typeof handle.world;` then `new World(seed, g)`, `new StateViews({ ...handle, world: w2 })`, and `w2.free()` when done. |
| Tick order | To match a `createGame` browser run, step first, then run rules: see [getting-started.md](../getting-started.md#tick-order). |

| Gotcha | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| A new level needs `--update` | Write the level and its `solution`, then `verify --update`; commit the `expect` it writes. A later engine or rule change that moves the hash fails `verify` until you check and re-pin it. |
| `par` | Must be at least the reference solution's part count, or `verify` fails the level. |
| One code path | Keep the sim free of DOM and timing so Node and the browser run identical code (`src/puzzle/sim.ts`). |
| Register it | New campaign levels are imported in `src/puzzle/levels.ts`. `--file` checks a loose file; pnpm runs the script in `apps/chain-reaction`, so pass an absolute path or one relative to that directory. |
| Schema | After changing `LevelSchema`, `pnpm --filter chain-reaction schema` rewrites `level.schema.json`. |
| Base prefabs | The `prefab` names a level uses (`block`, `ball`...) live in `levels/base.json`. |

See it in: [apps/chain-reaction/src/cli/verify.ts](../../apps/chain-reaction/src/cli/verify.ts) (lines 99-145), [apps/chain-reaction/src/puzzle/compose.ts](../../apps/chain-reaction/src/puzzle/compose.ts) (`composeLevel`, lines 152-256), [apps/chain-reaction/src/puzzle/level.ts](../../apps/chain-reaction/src/puzzle/level.ts) (`LevelSchema`, lines 38-104), [apps/chain-reaction/src/puzzle/node-engine.ts](../../apps/chain-reaction/src/puzzle/node-engine.ts).


===== docs/cookbook/assets-and-licensing.md =====

# Assets and licensing

Goal: add a model, HDRI, splat or texture that every app can load, without committing the file and with its licence recorded.

Large assets live in `apps/playground/public/assets/` (gitignored) and are fetched by `pnpm fetch-assets` from `apps/playground/assets.manifest.json`. Add an entry:

```json
{
	"id": "character-robot-expressive",
	"url": "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mrdoob/three.js/r170/examples/models/gltf/RobotExpressive/RobotExpressive.glb",
	"sha256": "047f5e5fb3bb6d378bd1df16ca6137f2a596c99b3a1b5690b4020c05aaf6f319",
	"license": "CC0 1.0",
	"attribution": "RobotExpressive by Tomás Laulhé (Quaternius, https://quaternius.com); modifications by Don McCurdy; distributed with three.js r170 examples",
	"file": "RobotExpressive.glb"
}
```

(one element of the manifest's `assets` array; it is not a scene). Then:

```bash
pnpm fetch-assets --update-hashes   # download what is missing, record every file's sha256 in the manifest
pnpm fetch-assets                   # verify every file; regenerates public/assets/LICENSES.md
```

Reference it from a scene as `"/assets/RobotExpressive.glb"` (`mesh.gltf.url`, `environment.hdri`, `environment.splat.url`). Commit the manifest and `LICENSES.md`, never the asset.

| Gotcha | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Licences | Only licences that allow commercial use: CC0, CC BY, MIT. CC BY-NC captures were rejected. Put the author, source and every modification in `attribution`. |
| Pin the URL | Use a commit- or release-pinned URL (`raw.githubusercontent.com/.../<sha>/...`) so the sha256 stays valid. |
| Hash mismatch | `--update-hashes` trusts whatever is on disk, so review the manifest diff: only your new entry should change. A cached file that does not match is re-fetched; if it still does not, it is deleted and the command fails. See [troubleshooting.md](../troubleshooting.md#fetch-assets-hash-mismatch-or-failed-avatar). |
| Derived assets | An entry with `derive` builds the file from `url` (checked against `sourceSha256`) with a pinned tool: `splat-transform` for splats (decimate under the 1.5M budget, convert to `.spz`), `scripts/assets/build-rocketbox.mjs` for the Rocketbox avatars. `sha256` is then the derived file's hash. |
| Every app sees them | Apps set `publicDir: "../playground/public"` in `vite.config.ts`, so `/assets/...` resolves in all of them. |
| Textures | glTF textures may be KTX2; the renderer's loader handles them with the Basis transcoder served at `/basis/` (copy an app's `vite.config.ts`). Load app-managed models with `game.renderer.loadGltf(url)`: cached per url and counted in `stats().textureMB`. |
| Serving under a sub-path | Root-absolute URLs (`/assets/...`, `/basis/`) in the scene, in `renderer.loadGltf` and in the transcoder path are prefixed with the asset base: `createGame({ assetBase })`, else `VITE_PEBBLE3D_ASSET_BASE` at build time, else Vite's `--base`, else `/` (unchanged). `vite build --base /x/` alone works because the public dir is copied under `/x/`; the public site shares one copy with `VITE_PEBBLE3D_ASSET_BASE=/pebble3d/`. For other app-loaded files use `renderer.assetUrl(url)`; `attachSound` does not resolve its URL, so pass it `renderer.assetUrl(url)`. |
| No file needed | Procedural geometry (Ronin Outpost's katana, `apps/katana-defense/src/game/view/katana.ts`) and synthesised audio need no manifest entry. |

See it in: [apps/playground/assets.manifest.json](../../apps/playground/assets.manifest.json), [apps/playground/public/assets/LICENSES.md](../../apps/playground/public/assets/LICENSES.md), [scripts/fetch-assets.mjs](../../scripts/fetch-assets.mjs), [apps/rockfall/vite.config.ts](../../apps/rockfall/vite.config.ts).


===== docs/cookbook/sub-path-hosting.md =====

# Sub-path hosting

Goal: serve a game from a URL like `https://example.com/games/skyrun/` instead of the site root, with every asset, the Basis transcoder and the wasm still loading.

Scenes and apps write shared files as root-absolute paths: `/assets/qwantani_noon_puresky_2k.hdr`, `/assets/rocketbox-male-adult-16.glb`, `/basis/`. The renderer prefixes those paths with an **asset base**, so the JSON never changes between a dev server at `/` and a build under a sub-path.

```bash
# from apps/<app>: everything (page, wasm, public assets, basis/) under /games/skyrun/
pnpm exec vite build --base /games/skyrun/
```

That is the whole change for a standalone build. Vite's `--base` (or `base: "/games/skyrun/"` in `vite.config.ts`) sets `import.meta.env.BASE_URL`, the renderer uses it as the asset base, and the build already contains what the prefixed URLs point at:

| URL in code | Resolves to | Served from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/assets/x.hdr` (scene `environment.hdri`, `splat.url`, glTF `mesh.gltf.url`, `renderer.loadGltf(url)`) | `/games/skyrun/assets/x.hdr` | `dist/assets/`, copied from the shared `publicDir: "../playground/public"` |
| `/basis/` (KTX2 transcoder, `createRenderer`'s `transcoderPath` default) | `/games/skyrun/basis/` | `dist/basis/`, emitted by the `basisTranscoder()` plugin in the copied `vite.config.ts` |
| `import detWasmUrl from ".../engine_core_det_bg.wasm?url"` | `/games/skyrun/assets/engine_core_det_bg-<hash>.wasm` | Vite rewrites `?url` imports for the base itself |
| `new Worker(new URL("./sim.worker.ts", import.meta.url), { type: "module" })` | under the base | Vite bundles the worker |

## Where the base comes from

First match wins (`packages/renderer/src/asset-base.ts`, `defaultAssetBase`):

1. `createGame({ assetBase })` or `createRenderer(canvas, settings, { assetBase })`.
2. `VITE_PEBBLE3D_ASSET_BASE`, an env var read at build time: the shared files live somewhere other than the game's own base.
3. Vite's `BASE_URL` (the `--base` the app was built with).
4. `"/"`: every URL is returned unchanged. Default builds and the dev server behave exactly as before.

`resolveAssetUrl(url, base)` (exported from `@pebble3d/renderer`) prefixes only root-absolute URLs. Relative URLs (`assets/x.glb`), protocol-relative `//host/x` and URLs with a scheme (`https:`, `data:`, `blob:`) pass through, and a URL that already starts with the base is not prefixed twice.

## Several games sharing one copy of the assets

`pnpm build:site` (`scripts/build-site.mjs`) builds every game in `site/src/data/games.json` this way:

```bash
VITE_PEBBLE3D_ASSET_BASE=/pebble3d/ VITE_PEBBLE3D_WEBGL_FALLBACK=1 \
  pnpm exec vite build --base /pebble3d/play/<id>/ --outDir site/dist/play/<id>
```

```text
site/dist/
  assets/          apps/playground/public/assets, copied once
  basis/           the Basis transcoder, kept once (LICENSE.txt added)
  play/<id>/       one game: index.html and its hashed bundles and wasm in assets/
```

The page, its JS and its wasm load from `/pebble3d/play/<id>/` (Vite's base); scene assets and the transcoder load from `/pebble3d/assets/` and `/pebble3d/basis/` (the asset base). After each game's build the script deletes that game's copies of the shared public files and of `basis/`, so the large splats and HDRIs exist once.

## What is not resolved for you

| You load | Do this |
| --- | --- |
| A file with your own `fetch`, `Audio`, `TextureLoader`, `HDRLoader` | Pass `renderer.assetUrl("/assets/x.ogg")` (the renderer's resolver with its base). |
| A sound through `attachSound` | It does not resolve its URL: `attachSound(..., renderer.assetUrl(url))`. |
| A glTF through your own `GLTFLoader` | Use `renderer.loadGltf(url)` instead: resolved, cached per url, KTX2-ready, counted in `stats().textureMB`. |
| A wasm URL posted to a Web Worker | Make it absolute first: `new URL(detWasmUrl, location.href).href`. A worker resolves a relative URL against its own script, not the page. |
| A link to another page of your site | `import.meta.env.BASE_URL + "other/"`. |

Without `createGame`, `createRenderer` applies the same default, so an app that boots itself (Skyrun, Swarm Siege) only needs root-absolute paths and the copied `vite.config.ts`.

## Check it

```bash
cd apps/<app>
pnpm exec vite build --base /x/   # into dist/ (gitignored)
ls dist                      # assets/ basis/ favicon.svg index.html
pnpm exec vite preview --base /x/ --port 5340   # open http://localhost:5340/x/
```

A 404 in the network tab names the URL that missed its base: usually a hand-written `fetch("/assets/...")` that should go through `renderer.assetUrl`.

| Gotcha | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Keep paths root-absolute | Write `/assets/x.glb`, not `assets/x.glb` or `./assets/x.glb`: relative paths are never prefixed and break on pages that are not at the base root. |
| Copy `vite.config.ts` | It is what serves `/basis/` in dev and emits `dist/basis/` on build; without it KTX2 textures fail under any base. (`apps/ringout` and `apps/drift-drone` load no KTX2 glTF and leave the plugin out, so their builds have no `basis/`.) |
| Don't prefix by hand | Leave paths root-absolute and let the asset base do it. A path you prefixed with `BASE_URL` yourself is wrong as soon as `VITE_PEBBLE3D_ASSET_BASE` points somewhere else. |

See it in: [apps/skyrun/src/main.ts](../../apps/skyrun/src/main.ts) (root-absolute HDRI, transcoder and runner glTFs with `createRenderer` and `renderer.loadGltf`, lines 86-115), [apps/swarm-siege/src/main.ts](../../apps/swarm-siege/src/main.ts) (absolute wasm URL for the sim worker, lines 109-112), [scripts/build-site.mjs](../../scripts/build-site.mjs) (the shared-assets layout, lines 76-137), [packages/renderer/src/asset-base.ts](../../packages/renderer/src/asset-base.ts).


===== docs/cookbook/custom-camera.md =====

# Custom camera

Goal: drive the camera from your own code (a chase cam, a fixed arena view, a top-down follow) without the built-in orbit controls fighting you for it.

## What the scene's `camera.controller` gives you

| `controller` | Created by `createRenderer` | Created by `createGame` | Input it takes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `"orbit"` (default) | `OrbitController` (three's `OrbitControls`) on the canvas, as `renderer.controller` | nothing more | Drag rotates, wheel zooms, right-drag pans; sets the canvas's `touch-action: none`. |
| `"fly"` | `FlyController`, as `renderer.controller` | nothing more | Keyboard and mouse fly-through. |
| `"thirdPerson"` | nothing: `renderer.controller` is `null` | a `ThirdPersonController` for the scene's first `character` (`game.player.camera`), or nothing when there is no character | Click to pointer-lock; mouse moves yaw and pitch. |

There is no `"none"` value. Two ways get you a camera nobody else moves:

- **Dispose the controller** after boot: `renderer.controller?.dispose(); renderer.controller = null;`. Works with any scene.
- **`"controller": "thirdPerson"` in a scene with no `character`**: no controller is ever created. Swarm Siege and Skyrun (which boot with `createRenderer`) do this.

Always call `dispose()` before setting `null`. Setting `renderer.controller = null` alone only stops the per-frame `update`; three's `OrbitControls` keeps its pointer and wheel listeners on the canvas, and those call `update()` themselves, so a drag still moves the camera between your writes.

## Drive it every frame

```ts
import type { Game } from "@pebble3d/sdk/game";
import { Vector3 } from "three/webgpu";

export function ownCamera(game: Game, targetId: string): void {
	const r = game.renderer;
	r.controller?.dispose(); // remove OrbitControls' canvas listeners
	r.controller = null;
	const cam = r.three.camera;
	cam.fov = 55;
	cam.updateProjectionMatrix(); // after any fov / near / far change

	const id = game.ids.get(targetId);
	if (id === undefined) throw new Error(`no "${targetId}" in the scene`);
	const slot = game.sim.world.slotOf(id);
	const focus = new Vector3();
	const want = new Vector3();
	let snap = true;

	game.onFrame((dt) => {
		const c = game.views.curr; // refreshed by createGame before onFrame
		want.set(c[slot * 8] as number, c[slot * 8 + 1] as number, c[slot * 8 + 2] as number);
		// Frame-rate independent easing; snap on the first frame.
		focus.lerp(want, snap ? 1 : 1 - Math.exp(-5 * dt));
		snap = false;
		cam.position.set(focus.x, focus.y + 12, focus.z + 9);
		cam.lookAt(focus);
	});
}
```

`onFrame` runs after `renderer.sync` (every visual is already at its interpolated pose) and before `renderer.render`, so a camera written there never lags a frame. To follow a visual rather than the raw tick state, read its object: `game.player.view.root.position` for the player character.

## A spring arm without the built-in rig

`ThirdPersonController` (from `@pebble3d/renderer`) works on its own: give it the camera and a ray function, call `update(pivot, dt)` each frame, and `connect(canvas)` if the mouse should steer it.

```ts
import { ThirdPersonController } from "@pebble3d/renderer";

const STATIC_ONLY = 1; // raycast filter: moving props never pull the arm in
const tpc = new ThirdPersonController(camera, (o, d, max) => {
	if (!world.raycast(o.x, o.y, o.z, d.x, d.y, d.z, max, STATIC_ONLY, 0)) return null;
	views.refresh(); // re-read scratch: wasm memory may have grown
	return views.scratch[0] as number;
});
tpc.distance = 6.4;
tpc.pitch = -0.3;
tpc.connect(canvas);
// per frame: tpc.update(pivot, dt); yaw 0 looks down -Z
```

| Gotcha | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Character movement follows the camera | `createGame` turns WASD into a world direction using `game.player.camera.yaw` when the rig has a third-person camera, else the yaw of `renderer.three.camera`. Owning the camera of a character scene with `"orbit"` plus `dispose()` keeps "W = away from the camera" working. With `"thirdPerson"`, setting `game.player.camera.enabled = false` stops it moving the camera, but movement still uses its (now frozen) yaw. |
| Presets and `pnpm shot --cam` | `game.setCamera("hero")` and `__pebble3d.setCamera` apply the preset straight to the camera when there is no controller, but your next `onFrame` overwrites it. Keep a flag and skip your camera code while a preset is active; replace `__pebble3d.setCamera` if the preset path must work in captures. |
| Shadow cascades | The sun's cascades are fitted to the camera frustum. `renderer.resize` refits them; after changing `fov`, `near` or `far` yourself, call `updateCsmFrustums(renderer.csm)` (exported from `@pebble3d/renderer`). |
| Things parented to the camera | The camera is not in the scene graph by default. `renderer.three.scene.add(camera)` before attaching a viewmodel or HUD mesh to it. |
| Camera collision | Cast with filter `1` (static only) as above; a dynamic prop in the ray makes the camera pop in and out. |

See it in: [apps/drift-drone/src/game/app.ts](../../apps/drift-drone/src/game/app.ts) (dispose the orbit controller and own the camera, lines 139-145) with [apps/drift-drone/src/game/view/camera-rig.ts](../../apps/drift-drone/src/game/view/camera-rig.ts) (chase cam kept out of walls by a static-only raycast, lines 71-120), [apps/ringout/src/game/app.ts](../../apps/ringout/src/game/app.ts) (lines 114-121), [apps/lanternfall/src/view/present.ts](../../apps/lanternfall/src/view/present.ts) (top-down follow of a character, lines 262-285), [apps/skyrun/src/game/view/camera-rig.ts](../../apps/skyrun/src/game/view/camera-rig.ts) (a standalone `ThirdPersonController`, lines 35-51), [apps/skyrun/src/main.ts](../../apps/skyrun/src/main.ts) (`setCamera` presets next to a game camera, lines 340-347), [apps/swarm-siege/scenes/plateau.json](../../apps/swarm-siege/scenes/plateau.json) (`"thirdPerson"` with no character, line 24).


===== docs/cookbook/owning-the-world.md =====

# Owning the world

Goal: keep `createGame` for the renderer, the canvas and the automation hook, but run your game in physics worlds your code creates, steps, draws and throws away (a fresh world per round, a replay world beside the live one, a level editor's Play button).

`createGame` loads one wasm module and makes one `World` for the scene. Any number of extra worlds can come from that same module:

```ts
import type { Game } from "@pebble3d/sdk/game";
import { type SimHandle, StateViews } from "@pebble3d/sdk/sim";
import { expandScene } from "@pebble3d/sdk/expand";
import { parseScene } from "@pebble3d/sdk/schema";

type World = SimHandle["world"];

export function worldMaker(h: SimHandle): (seed: number, gravity: number) => World {
	const Ctor = h.world.constructor as new (seed: number, gravity: number) => World;
	return (seed, gravity) => new Ctor(seed, gravity);
}

export class Round {
	readonly world: World;
	readonly views: StateViews;
	readonly ids: Map<string, number>;
	tick = 0;

	constructor(game: Game, sceneJson: unknown) {
		const scene = parseScene(sceneJson);
		this.world = worldMaker(game.sim)(scene.sim.seed, scene.sim.gravity);
		this.ids = new Map();
		for (const e of expandScene(scene).sim)
			this.ids.set(e.sceneId, this.world.spawn(JSON.stringify(e.desc)));
		// StateViews only needs the world and the module's memory.
		this.views = new StateViews({ ...game.sim, world: this.world });
		this.world.step(1); // raycasts see nothing until the first step
		this.tick = 1;
		this.views.refresh();
	}

	step(): void {
		// rules that write forces / kinematic poses go here, then:
		this.world.step(1);
		this.tick++;
		this.views.refresh();
	}

	free(): void {
		this.world.free();
	}
}
```

## Step it from `onFrame`

`createGame` keeps stepping its own (now idle) world; your world advances only when you call `step()`. Run it on an accumulator fed by `onFrame`'s `dt`:

```ts
const DT = 1 / 60;
let acc = 0;
game.onFrame((dt) => {
	acc += dt;
	let n = 0;
	while (acc >= DT - 1e-9 && n < 5) {
		acc -= DT;
		round.step();
		n++;
	}
	if (n === 5) acc = 0; // drop the backlog instead of spiralling
	view.sync(round, Math.min(1, acc / DT)); // alpha for interpolation
});
```

In fixed mode `onFrame`'s `dt` is exactly `1/60` per frame and 0 once `stopAtTick` is reached, so this runs one tick per frame and stops with `createGame`'s world: `pnpm shot --ticks n` still captures your world at tick n (plus the step in the constructor, if you keep it).

## Draw its bodies

The renderer only draws `createGame`'s world: `renderer.sync` and `renderer.instances` read `game.views`, whose slots mean nothing for your world. Build your own meshes and place them from your views with `readSlot` (from `@pebble3d/renderer`), which interpolates and honours `NO_INTERP`:

```ts
import { primitiveGeometry, readSlot } from "@pebble3d/renderer";
import { Mesh, MeshStandardNodeMaterial, Quaternion, Vector3 } from "three/webgpu";

const _p = new Vector3();
const _q = new Quaternion();

export class RoundView {
	private readonly items: { mesh: Mesh; slot: number }[] = [];

	add(game: Game, round: Round, id: string, size: [number, number, number]): void {
		const mesh = new Mesh(primitiveGeometry("box", size), new MeshStandardNodeMaterial());
		mesh.castShadow = true;
		game.renderer.three.scene.add(mesh);
		const simId = round.ids.get(id) as number;
		this.items.push({ mesh, slot: round.world.slotOf(simId) });
	}

	sync(round: Round, alpha: number): void {
		const { prev, curr } = round.views;
		for (const it of this.items) {
			const on = it.slot >= 0 && readSlot(prev, curr, it.slot, alpha, _p, _q);
			it.mesh.visible = on; // false once the slot is freed
			if (on) {
				it.mesh.position.copy(_p);
				it.mesh.quaternion.copy(_q);
			}
		}
	}
}
```

`primitiveGeometry(primitive, size)` builds the same geometry the renderer uses for scene primitives, at the real size. For many identical bodies, one `InstancedMesh` you fill from the slots is cheaper than one mesh each.

## Report your world to automation

`pnpm shot` writes `__pebble3d.stateHash()` into the sidecar, and `createGame` installs it for **its** world. Point it at yours, or every capture reports the same idle hash:

```ts
Object.assign(window.__pebble3d ?? {}, {
	stateHash: () => round.world.stateHash(),
	game: { tick: () => round.tick },
});
```

| Gotcha | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| One memory for every world | All worlds from one module share one `WebAssembly.Memory`. A `spawn` in *any* world (createGame's included) can grow it, which detaches every `Float32Array` over the old buffer: views of other worlds read zeros (`byteLength` 0). Call `views.refresh()` after spawning or stepping, and read `views.curr` / `views.scratch` from the object each time instead of keeping the array in a local or a field. |
| Scratch after a query | Query results land in the shared scratch region. Read them right after the call, through `views.scratch` after a `refresh()` (cheap: it compares four numbers and returns). |
| Raycasts on a new world | A world that has never stepped has an empty query structure: every `raycast` returns false, even onto a static floor. Step once after spawning (as above) before probing. Bodies spawned later are likewise invisible to raycasts until the next step. |
| Free what you make | `world.free()` when a round ends; wasm memory is not garbage-collected. |
| Same seed, same order | Spawn order and seed decide the state hash; spawning from `expandScene(scene).sim` in order matches `createGame` and Node. |
| Keep the scene small | `createGame` still needs a valid scene: an environment and a camera preset are enough. Its world steps every frame, so leave dynamic bodies out of it. |
| The camera | The orbit controller is still on the canvas; see [custom-camera.md](custom-camera.md). |
| Node | The same `Round` class runs in a test with `loadSim("deterministic", bytes)` as the handle, so the browser and the verifier call one code path. |

See it in: [apps/pebble-garden/src/garden/sim.ts](../../apps/pebble-garden/src/garden/sim.ts) (worlds from the loaded module, lines 43-46; spawn from `expandScene` and views, lines 133-186; one tick, lines 221-237) with [apps/pebble-garden/src/view/garden-view.ts](../../apps/pebble-garden/src/view/garden-view.ts) (meshes from `primitiveGeometry`, placed with `readSlot`, lines 165-176), [apps/ringout/src/game/physics.ts](../../apps/ringout/src/game/physics.ts) (world factory and views that re-point after growth, lines 15-70), [apps/ringout/src/game/app.ts](../../apps/ringout/src/game/app.ts) (accumulator in `onFrame`, lines 491-503; alpha, lines 563-569), [apps/ringout/src/main.ts](../../apps/ringout/src/main.ts) (`stateHash` override, lines 95-99), [apps/pebble-garden/src/main.ts](../../apps/pebble-garden/src/main.ts) (lines 182-186), [apps/lanternfall/src/game/sim.ts](../../apps/lanternfall/src/game/sim.ts) (raycast work deferred to the first tick, lines 325-329).


===== skills/make-a-game/SKILL.md =====

---
name: make-a-game
description: Use when a developer asks for a game, a game prototype or a playable demo built with Pebble3D (for example "make me a game where...", "build a racing game", "prototype this idea"). Start here before writing any game code.
---

# Make a game

The front door for every game request in this repo. It fixes the order of work and the check that ends each step. The other skills hold the how; this one holds the sequence. Follow it in order and do not skip ahead to code.

Assumptions: you are in a clone of the Pebble3D monorepo, the game becomes a new app in `apps/<name>/` like the demos in `apps/`, and the repo is set up (`pnpm i && pnpm build:wasm`, see [docs/getting-started.md](../../docs/getting-started.md)). The working rules for the repo are in [AGENTS.md](../../AGENTS.md).

## The sequence

interview → brief → scaffold → build → game feel → art pass → complete loop → verify

| Step          | Load                                                                                                                      | Exit check before moving on                                                                                                                       |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Interview     | [game-interview](../game-interview/SKILL.md)                                                                              | Every open question is answered, defaulted, or written down as an assumption.                                                                     |
| Brief         | [game-interview](../game-interview/SKILL.md) (its last section)                                                           | `apps/<name>/BRIEF.md` exists and the developer said yes to it (or, non-interactive, its assumptions are marked).                                 |
| Scaffold      | [start-a-game](../start-a-game/SKILL.md)                                                                                  | `pnpm --filter <name> dev` serves the scene, the first capture shows it (not black), zero console errors, `npx vitest run --project <name>` runs. |
| Build         | [engine-pitfalls](../engine-pitfalls/SKILL.md), then [genre-playbooks](../genre-playbooks/SKILL.md) for the closest genre | The core verbs from the brief work with the keyboard, the `?demo=1` bot performs them, and sim tests pass.                                        |
| Game feel     | [game-feel](../game-feel/SKILL.md)                                                                                        | Every player action has visible and audible feedback; a capture sequence shows it.                                                                |
| Art pass      | [art-direction](../art-direction/SKILL.md)                                                                                | Captures match the "look" section of the brief; palette, lighting and post are one committed style, not defaults.                                 |
| Complete loop | [complete-game-loop](../complete-game-loop/SKILL.md)                                                                      | Title → play → win or lose → results → restart works by keyboard and by the `?demo=1` bot; README lists controls and URL params.                  |
| Verify        | [verify-your-work](../verify-your-work/SKILL.md)                                                                          | Everything in that skill passes. **`verify-your-work` defines done; never report done without it.**                                               |

Load [verify-your-work](../verify-your-work/SKILL.md) early too: run its quick checks (a capture, the console, the tests) at the end of every step from scaffold on, not only at the end. A step whose capture you have not looked at is not finished.

Load [engine-pitfalls](../engine-pitfalls/SKILL.md) whenever something renders black, throws, times out in a capture, or behaves differently in Node and the browser. Look up the symptom there and in [docs/troubleshooting.md](../../docs/troubleshooting.md) before debugging from scratch.

## What the developer may skip

The developer decides; you do not skip on their behalf.

- **Interview**: "just build it", or a request that already answers what the player does, the look, controls, players and scope. You still write `BRIEF.md`, with the defaults listed under assumptions, and show it.
- **Developer approval of the brief**: only when they said not to wait. Then proceed on the assumptions and say so in your first progress message.
- **Game feel, art pass**: only for an explicitly throwaway prototype ("just the mechanic, grey boxes are fine"). Record the skip in `BRIEF.md` under out of scope.
- **Complete loop**: the same rule; a mechanic test may stop at "play". Keep the `?demo=1` bot anyway, because verification drives it.
- **Never skippable**: scaffold, build, and verify. A game that was not captured, looked at and tested is not delivered.

If the developer changes direction mid-way, update `BRIEF.md` first, then continue from the earliest step the change affects.

## Working habits

- One step at a time. Finish its exit check, tell the developer in one or two lines what now works, then load the next skill.
- Show, do not describe: when a step changes what is on screen, share the capture with the progress message.
- Study before inventing. The demos in `apps/` solve most problems a new game hits; [docs/examples.md](../../docs/examples.md) lists what each one shows, and the cookbook in [docs/cookbook/](../../docs/cookbook/README.md) has the recipes.
- Keep the repo invariants from [AGENTS.md](../../AGENTS.md): seeded randomness only in the sim (no `Math.random` or `Date`), no per-frame allocation, no engine changes. If the game needs an engine feature, tell the developer instead of editing `packages/` or `crates/`.
- Original work only: never name, copy or imitate an existing commercial game, its characters or its art.
- Online multiplayer is not available (the engine has no netcode). Offer local multiplayer on one keyboard or bot opponents, as `apps/ringout` does.

## Reporting done

Only after `verify-your-work` passes, report: what was built (link `BRIEF.md`), how to run it (`pnpm --filter <name> dev` and the URL), the controls, the captures you looked at, test results, and any assumption or skip still open.


===== skills/game-interview/SKILL.md =====

---
name: game-interview
description: Use when a game request leaves open what the player does, how it should feel or look, the controls, the players or the scope, and you need a short design brief the developer approves before any code is written.
---

# Game interview

Turn a request ("a game where you bounce enemies off the edge") into `apps/<name>/BRIEF.md`, a one-page brief the developer says yes to. The goal is to learn what they picture, not to fill a form. Next: `start-a-game`.

## Rules

- **At most six questions, one per message.** Wait for the answer before the next.
- **Ask only what the request leaves open.** If they said "racing game with a drone", do not ask what the player does.
- **Propose, do not interrogate.** Once you know _why_ they want the game, offer a concrete default and let them correct it: "I'd make it one screen, top-down camera, three lives. Sound right?" beats "How many lives?".
- **Biggest unknown first.** Usually the look or what the player does. A good opener restates the request in one sentence, then asks one open question about the vaguest word in it: "When you say very stylized, what do you picture?"
- **Show, when the look is their call.** Words fail for visuals; see "Mockups" below.
- Never name or suggest imitating an existing commercial game. If the developer names one, ask what they like about it (the feel, the camera, the pace) and write that down instead of the title.
- Keep a running list of what you have decided. That list becomes the brief.

## The six topics

In rough priority order. Skip any the request or an earlier answer already settles.

| Topic                | What you need                                                                | Default to propose if they shrug                                                 |
| -------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| What the player does | The core verbs (roll, dash, jump, place, shoot) and the goal of a round      | One verb plus one special move, a round that ends in a win or a loss             |
| The feel             | Pace and weight: floaty or heavy, frantic or calm, forgiving or punishing    | Responsive and weighty, short rounds, quick restart                              |
| The look             | Style, palette, mood, camera; what it should remind them of (in their words) | One committed style suggested by the theme (for example toon with bold outlines) |
| Controls, platform   | Keyboard, mouse, gamepad, touch; desktop or phone browser                    | Keyboard on a desktop browser                                                    |
| Players              | Single player, local multiplayer on one keyboard, or online                  | Single player against bots                                                       |
| Scope of v1          | What the first playable version contains, and what waits                     | One arena or level, the full loop (title, play, results, restart)                |

**Players:** the engine has no online netcode. If they want online play, say so plainly and offer local multiplayer on one keyboard, bot opponents, or both, as `apps/ringout` does ([its README](../../apps/ringout/README.md)). Put online play under out of scope.

## Mockups

When the look (or a visual effect) is the developer's call and they cannot describe it, offer to show options instead of asking:

1. Write a throwaway HTML page outside the app (a temp folder is fine) with a few small animated variants side by side: for example four hit-effect styles, three palettes, or two camera angles. Label each with a letter.
2. Open it in their browser and ask which one is closest, or what to mix.
3. If they pick one and want more detail, make a second, more detailed page of that one.
4. When the choice depends on how it looks in the real renderer, do a quick in-engine test: a scene file in `apps/playground/scenes/` captured with `pnpm shot --scene <name>` (the file name without `.json`; see [docs/getting-started.md](../../docs/getting-started.md)). Delete the test scene afterwards.

Keep mockups cheap: minutes, not hours. They decide a direction; they are not the game.

## Non-interactive or "just build it"

If you cannot hold a back-and-forth (a headless run, a tool without replies) or the developer says "just build it":

1. If you can send one message and get one reply, ask all your open questions in that single message, each with the default you will use, so they can answer only the ones they care about.
2. If there is no reply, or they said "just build it", use the defaults from the table above (adjusted to whatever the request did say).
3. Write `BRIEF.md` anyway, with every default listed under **Assumptions**, and continue without waiting for approval. Mention the assumptions in your first progress message so the developer can correct them.

## Writing the brief

1. Pick the app name: short, lowercase, hyphenated, original (not a commercial title), and not already a folder in `apps/`. It is also the package name and the `--filter` name.
2. Copy [brief-template.md](brief-template.md) to `apps/<name>/BRIEF.md` (create the folder; `start-a-game` fills in the rest). Fill every section in the developer's words where you can. Keep it to one page.
3. Show it to the developer: "Here is the brief. Yes, or what should change?" Edit until they say yes.
4. Exit check: `BRIEF.md` exists, has no empty sections, and is approved (or its assumptions are marked, in the non-interactive case).


===== skills/start-a-game/SKILL.md =====

---
name: start-a-game
description: Use when creating a new game app under apps/ in the Pebble3D repo, before writing gameplay code, to scaffold it the way the demos are laid out and prove it boots, captures and runs its tests.
---

# Start a game

Scaffold `apps/<name>/` so it builds, serves, captures and tests like the demos do, before any gameplay exists. `<name>` is the app name from `apps/<name>/BRIEF.md`. Next: build the game (`make-a-game` says which skill).

The full walkthrough with every file is [docs/getting-started.md](../../docs/getting-started.md) (section "A minimal game app"). This skill is the checklist and the template to copy.

## Template: Ringout

Copy the layout of `apps/ringout`, a small, complete game (title, play, results, rematch, bot, captures). Read these before copying:

| File                                                                | Take from it                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [package.json](../../apps/ringout/package.json)                     | Scripts `dev` (with `--port <n> --strictPort`), `build`, `preview`, `test`, `typecheck`; deps `@pebble3d/sdk`, `@pebble3d/renderer` (`workspace:*`) and the pinned `three`. Change `name` and the port.                                                                             |
| [vite.config.ts](../../apps/ringout/vite.config.ts)                 | `publicDir: "../playground/public"`, `appType: "mpa"`, `server.fs.allow`, the env var for the build base. Rename the env var. If the game loads glTF or KTX2, copy [apps/rockfall/vite.config.ts](../../apps/rockfall/vite.config.ts) instead: it adds the Basis transcoder plugin. |
| [index.html](../../apps/ringout/index.html)                         | `<canvas id="app">`, a HUD root, the favicon link, the module script.                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| [src/main.ts](../../apps/ringout/src/main.ts)                       | URL params documented in the top comment and parsed strictly; `createGame` with both wasm `?url` imports, `mode`, `backend`, `stopAtTick`; `window.__pebble3d` probes; `main().catch` writing `__pebble3d.error`.                                                                   |
| [README.md](../../apps/ringout/README.md)                           | Sections: what it is, Run it (commands and a URL param table), Controls, What it shows off, Known issues.                                                                                                                                                                           |
| [bench/capture-final.sh](../../apps/ringout/bench/capture-final.sh) | Build once, then one `pnpm shot` per moment with `--no-build`, a fixed `--port`, `--param demo=1`; stops on the first failure.                                                                                                                                                      |

Also copy `tsconfig.json` and `vitest.config.ts` from `apps/ringout/` (change the project `name`). Keep game code under `src/game/` (sim, bot, input, UI) and scenes under `scenes/`. Start with the smallest scene that shows something: a ground, a light preset, one player body.

## Checklist

1. **Folder and files.** Create the files above in `apps/<name>/`. `BRIEF.md` is already there from `game-interview`; do not overwrite it.
2. **Pick an unused port.** List the ports in use:

   ```bash
   grep -rhoE -- '--port[ =][[:digit:]]+' apps/*/package.json apps/*/bench | sort -u
   ```

   Pick a free one for `dev` (keep `--strictPort`, so a clash fails loudly instead of moving), and a different free one for the capture script's `--port`. Ringout uses 5270 for dev and 5271 for captures. Note the default playground dev server uses 5173.
3. **Register the tests.** Add `"apps/<name>"` to the `projects` array in the root `vitest.config.ts`, next to the other apps. Without it the app's tests never run and `--project <name>` matches nothing.
4. **Demo mode.** Parse `?demo=1` in `src/main.ts` and drive the game with a bot that writes the same input a player produces. At this stage the bot can be trivial (press start, move toward something); it grows with the game. See [docs/cookbook/demo-bot-and-captures.md](../../docs/cookbook/demo-bot-and-captures.md).
5. **Fixed-tick mode.** Read `mode` and `ticks` and pass `stopAtTick`, or every `pnpm shot` times out.
6. **WebGL fallback.** `createGame` already honours `?webglFallback=1` (see [docs/troubleshooting.md](../../docs/troubleshooting.md)): do not pass `webglFallback: false`, and support `?backend=webgl` like Ringout does. Check both URLs load.
7. **Sub-path builds.** Keep asset URLs root-absolute (`/assets/...`) and build URLs in code from `import.meta.env.BASE_URL`, so the game can be hosted under a sub-path: [docs/cookbook/sub-path-hosting.md](../../docs/cookbook/sub-path-hosting.md).
8. **Install.** Run `pnpm install` at the repo root so pnpm links the workspace packages.
9. **A first test.** One Node test in `test/` that loads the scene and steps the sim with the real wasm (pattern in [docs/getting-started.md](../../docs/getting-started.md), "Tests in Node").

## Exit check

All of these, before any gameplay work. The dev server never exits, so start it in the background or a second terminal (not in the same shell before the other commands, which would block), and leave it running while you open the pages:

```bash
npx vitest run --project <name>          # runs your test (not "No projects were found")
pnpm --filter <name> typecheck
pnpm shot --app <name> --param demo=1 --ticks 120 --name first
pnpm --filter <name> dev &               # background; open http://localhost:<port>/ and /?demo=1
```

- The shot exits 0, its `.json` sidecar has an empty `console` array, and you opened the PNG whose path the shot prints: the scene is visible, not black or empty.
- `?webglFallback=1` and `?backend=webgl` load without errors.
- `pnpm lint` is clean for the new files.

If the shot fails or the frame is black, look up the symptom in [docs/troubleshooting.md](../../docs/troubleshooting.md) (stale wasm after a pull is the usual cause: `pnpm build:wasm`).


===== skills/verify-your-work/SKILL.md =====

---
name: verify-your-work
description: Use when a Pebble3D game or app change looks finished, at the end of every make-a-game step from scaffold on, or before telling anyone a game works. Defines done: tests, captures, sidecars, looking at every image, both backends.
---

# Verify your work

This skill is the definition of done. A game is not done because it compiles or because a capture exited 0. It is done when the checks below pass and you have looked at what the player will see. Never report done without it.

The reference for every command and flag is [docs/verification.md](../../docs/verification.md). The demo bot and capture script pattern is [docs/cookbook/demo-bot-and-captures.md](../../docs/cookbook/demo-bot-and-captures.md). Any failure: look it up in [docs/troubleshooting.md](../../docs/troubleshooting.md) before debugging from scratch.

`<name>` below is the app folder under `apps/`.

## Quick checks (end of every step)

Run these at the end of every [make-a-game](../make-a-game/SKILL.md) step from scaffold on. They take a minute and catch most regressions.

```bash
npx vitest run --project <name>
pnpm shot --app <name> --param demo=1 --ticks 600 --name check
```

1. The tests pass, and the output shows your test files ran (not "No test files found").
2. The shot exits 0. Its last line names the backend, adapter, tick and `stateHash`.
3. Open the `.json` sidecar next to the PNG and read it (next section).
4. Open the PNG whose path the shot prints, and look at it (the section after).

A step whose capture you have not opened is not finished.

## Read the sidecar

Every capture writes a `.json` sidecar beside the PNG. Check each field; a capture that exits 0 can still be wrong.

| Field         | Pass when                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `console`     | An empty array. Never allowlist your own errors to get there; fix them. A warning counts too: fix it, or explain it in the README's known issues with the reason. Never leave one silent.                                       |
| `adapterInfo` | `backend` is the one you asked for, and the device names a real GPU, not SwiftShader or llvmpipe.                                                                                                                               |
| `tick`        | The tick you asked for with `--ticks`.                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| `stateHash`   | Different between captures of different moments in a game that moves. The same hash everywhere means the hook reports an idle world: [stateHash never changes](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#the-shot-statehash-never-changes). |
| `game`        | Your `__pebble3d.game` probes read what the frame should show: the phase (title, playing, results), the bot's current action, score.                                                                                            |

Run the same capture twice: the `stateHash` must match. If it does not, the sim is not deterministic: [determinism hash mismatch](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#determinism-hash-mismatch).

## Look at every image

Open every PNG (and the animated WebP from a `--sequence`) with your image viewer or file reader. Exit 0 only means nothing errored. For each one, check and write down:

- **Not blank.** Not black, not white, not a flat sky with nothing in it. A black or white frame on WebGL only: [WebGL outdoor black/white](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#webgl-outdoor-scene-is-black-or-white).
- **The subject is in frame.** The player, the goal and the threat are visible and readable at a glance, not hidden behind scenery or off screen.
- **The moment is the one you meant.** The title capture shows the title, the results capture shows results. If not, move the tick (scout it headless, as the cookbook's "Scout ticks headless" row explains).
- **The HUD is readable.** Text not clipped or overlapping, contrast against the scene, numbers that make sense.
- **It matches the brief.** The palette, lighting and mood in the "look" section of `apps/<name>/BRIEF.md`, not engine defaults.
- **No rendering faults.** Flickering or z-fighting surfaces, stretched textures, floating or sunken objects, characters in a bind pose.

Describe what you saw in one line per image in your report. If you cannot describe it, you did not look. Reading the `.json` sidecar is not looking: the sidecar cannot show a black frame, a clipped HUD or the wrong moment. Every PNG and WebP you captured gets opened and gets its own line, including the ones from the capture script and the WebGL run.

## The full check (before reporting done)

All of these pass, in this order.

1. **Unit and sim tests.** `npx vitest run --project <name>`. The app has a determinism test written like `apps/rockfall/test/sim.test.ts`: the same seed and input log run twice give the same `world.stateHash()`, and one changed input gives a different one.
2. **Types and lint.** `pnpm typecheck` and `pnpm lint`. Lint must add no new warnings for your files.
3. **The capture script.** `bash apps/<name>/bench/capture-final.sh` exits 0. It covers at least title, mid-play, a win or loss, the results screen and one `--sequence` of the core action, all driven by the `?demo=1` bot. Read every sidecar and look at every image, as above.
4. **The demo bot plays the whole loop.** The captures and the `game` probes show it reaching results and restarting, with the same input type a player produces.
5. **The WebGL path.** WebGPU is not everywhere: Firefox, Safari and many Linux Chromium builds get WebGL. Capture with `--backend webgl` and look at it; it must exit 0 and look like the WebGPU capture. Then load the game with `?webglFallback=1`, headed (the dev server in a browser) or headless (`pnpm shot --app <name> --param webglFallback=1 --param demo=1 --name fallback`), and check it boots and plays with no console errors; do the same for `/?backend=webgl`. `createGame` reads `webglFallback` from the URL by itself; never pass `webglFallback: false`.
6. **Performance, when you claim it.** Build, then run the app's fps bench on an idle GPU, on both backends, in a browser that reached the real GPU. Numbers from a headless run on SwiftShader, or from one backend only, prove nothing: [misleading fps](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fps-from-a-headless-or-webgl-run-is-misleading) and [low or noisy fps](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fps-numbers-are-low-or-noisy). The target is 60 fps.
7. **Engine determinism, only if engine code changed.** Games should not change `packages/` or `crates/`. If something did change there, run `pnpm build:wasm` and the determinism script from [AGENTS.md](../../AGENTS.md); it must print `2d76d9927e780425`.
8. **The README.** `apps/<name>/README.md` lists how to run it, the controls and every URL param the game reads (including `demo`, `seed`, `mode`, `ticks`, `backend`), and a known-issues section for any console warning you could not fix, each with its reason.

### Exit lines for the full check

Each of these is a line you can write truthfully in your report, or the check is not done:

- **Every capture opened.** I opened every PNG and WebP I captured (not only the sidecars), and my report has one line per capture saying what it shows.
- **WebGL fallback loaded.** I loaded the game with `?webglFallback=1` (headed or headless) and it booted and played with no console errors.
- **No silent console messages.** Every console error and warning from every capture and page load is fixed, or listed in the README's known issues with the reason.

## When headless WebGPU has no adapter

The right action depends on the symptom.

1. **`software/fallback adapter (SwiftShader) refused`** (often after `shot: headless got a software adapter; retrying headed`). Only this case retries: `pnpm shot` tries once more in a visible window, and only with a display (`DISPLAY` or `WAYLAND_DISPLAY` set). Pass `--headed` to go straight there. Details: [SwiftShader adapter](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#shot-refuses-a-swiftshader-adapter).
2. **`BackendUnavailable: webgpu (WebGPURenderer fell back to WebGL)` or `requested backend webgpu but the page ran webgl`.** The shot does not retry these; headed alone will not help. Open `chrome://gpu` in the same Chromium and read the WebGPU line. On Linux, WebGPU is often off: launch with `--enable-unsafe-webgpu --enable-features=Vulkan --use-angle=vulkan` (`pnpm shot` already does). Details: [BackendUnavailable: webgpu](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#backendunavailable-webgpu). To check the fallback itself rather than WebGPU, capture with `--param webglFallback=1` or `--backend webgl`; that is a WebGL check and does not stand in for the WebGPU capture.
3. **Your own boot must report the adapter.** A custom boot without `createGame` has to fill `__pebble3d.adapterInfo`, or the software check cannot work: [SwiftShader adapter](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#shot-refuses-a-swiftshader-adapter).
4. **No GPU at all** (a container, a remote shell without a display): you cannot verify rendering there. Still run the Node tests, typecheck and lint, then tell the developer plainly that no capture was taken and why, and ask them to run the capture script on a machine with a GPU. Do not switch to WebGL on SwiftShader, allowlist the error, or describe images you did not see.

## Reporting done

Report only after the full check passes:

- What was built, with a link to `apps/<name>/BRIEF.md`.
- How to run it: `pnpm --filter <name> dev` and the URL, plus the controls.
- Test, typecheck and lint results, as the commands printed them.
- The captures you looked at, each with the PNG path the shot printed and your one-line description of it.
- Which backends you checked, and fps only if you measured it as above.
- Anything skipped or still open, and every assumption from the brief that the developer has not confirmed.

If any check failed and you could not fix it, say which one and what you saw. A precise "not done yet" is worth more than a false "done".


===== skills/engine-pitfalls/SKILL.md =====

---
name: engine-pitfalls
description: Use when building gameplay with Pebble3D, and whenever something renders black, throws, times out in a capture, or behaves differently in Node and the browser. Known engine traps as "if you see X, do Y", each linked to the full fix.
---

# Engine pitfalls

Traps that cost the demo builders hours. Read the whole list once before the build step of [make-a-game](../make-a-game/SKILL.md), then come back by symptom. Each line says what to do; the link has the cause and the full fix in [docs/troubleshooting.md](../../docs/troubleshooting.md). Do not debug from scratch before checking here.

## Rendering

- **`BackendUnavailable: webgpu`** → the browser has no WebGPU. Open with `?webglFallback=1` or `?backend=webgl`, or launch Chromium with the WebGPU flags; check `chrome://gpu`. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#backendunavailable-webgpu)
- **Outdoor scene black or white on WebGL only** → load HDRIs through the engine's environment loader, not your own PMREM. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#webgl-outdoor-scene-is-black-or-white)
- **Your camera drifts when the mouse drags or scrolls** → dispose the default orbit controller after boot and set it to null. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#the-orbit-camera-fights-your-camera)
- **A second character slides in its bind pose** → only the player gets an animated view; attach the others yourself. Entity order picks the player. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#other-characters-do-not-animate)
- **A teleported static body's mesh stays put** → anything that moves must be `"kinematic"`. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#a-static-mesh-does-not-move)
- **Night or interior scene looks like daylight** → lower the scene's `environmentIntensity` and add a fixed pool of three.js point lights; the schema has only a sun. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#a-night-scene-is-too-bright)
- **Draw calls jump with each character** → shadow casters draw once per cascade; turn shadows off for props, crowds and decals. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#draw-calls-climb-with-each-character)
- **Toon ink lines around decals on a splat floor** → make the decals transparent materials. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#decals-on-a-splat-floor-get-ink-outlines)
- **Two captures of the same tick differ by a few pixels** → normal GPU noise; compare `stateHash`, not bytes. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#two-identical-shots-differ-slightly)

## Physics and sim

- **`world.setVelocity is not a function`, or a feature silently does nothing after a pull** → stale wasm: `pnpm build:wasm`, restart the dev server. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#stale-wasm-setvelocity-is-not-a-function)
- **Determinism hash mismatch** → stale wasm first, then `Math.random`/`Date`/wall-clock `dt` in the sim, then the `fast` build. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#determinism-hash-mismatch)
- **Node test hash differs from the browser at the same tick** → mirror the browser tick order exactly: physics step, refresh views, bot, rules. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#headless-hash-differs-from-the-browser)
- **Bot or rules input ignored on high-refresh displays** → re-send your character input at the end of every frame, after the tick loop. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#your-setcharacterinput-is-overwritten)
- **Reads return zeros after a spawn** → a spawn detached the views; call `views.refresh()` and read through the views object. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#state-views-read-zeros-after-a-spawn)
- **Raycast misses on a world you just built** → step once before the first query. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#raycasts-miss-on-a-new-world)
- **You want collision callbacks** → there are none; detect contacts in your rules from distances and velocities. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#there-are-no-contact-events)
- **A ball rolls forever** → set `angularDamping` on rolling bodies. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#spheres-roll-forever)
- **The game crawls under heavy physics** → cap ticks per frame, consider the `fast` build or a worker. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#heavy-physics-makes-the-game-crawl)
- **You need a per-tick hook or runtime spawns** → `createGame` has neither; advance your own sim in `onFrame` or boot like Rockfall. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#creategame-has-no-per-tick-hook)
- **Level switch leaves the old game running** → one game per page; new worlds inside it, or reload with new params. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#a-second-game-on-the-same-page)
- **Scene errors appear one per run** → validate with `SceneSchema.safeParse` and print every issue. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#only-the-first-scene-error-is-reported)
- **`TS2352` on an imported scene JSON** → cast through `unknown`. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#ts2352-when-passing-an-imported-scene-json)

## Assets and hosting

- **404 for `/favicon.ico` or an asset fails a capture** → add the favicon link, run `pnpm fetch-assets`, copy a demo's `vite.config.ts`. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#shot-fails-on-a-404)
- **Assets, transcoder or wasm 404 under a sub-path** → keep URLs root-absolute and pass hand-loaded ones through `renderer.assetUrl`. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#assets-404-under-a-sub-path)
- **`fetch-assets` hash mismatch or failed avatar** → check the download; the avatar build is linux-x64 only. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fetch-assets-hash-mismatch-or-failed-avatar)

## Captures, benches and toolchain

- **Shot times out on `__pebble3d.done`** → read `mode` and `ticks` from the URL and pass `stopAtTick`; catch boot errors into `__pebble3d.error`. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#shot-times-out-waiting-for-__pebble3ddone)
- **Shot refuses a SwiftShader adapter** → run where a real GPU and a display exist, or `--headed`; a custom boot must report its adapter. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#shot-refuses-a-swiftshader-adapter)
- **`--out must be inside` the capture folder** → omit `--out`, or keep it under the default capture folder. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#shot---out-rejected)
- **Sidecar `stateHash` never changes** → point `__pebble3d.stateHash` at the world your game really runs. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#the-shot-statehash-never-changes)
- **Fixed-mode captures flaky with a worker sim** → run the sim inline in fixed mode, the worker only in realtime. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fixed-mode-captures-with-a-worker-sim)
- **fps looks good headless, or only WebGL was measured** → confirm a real GPU renderer string and measure both backends. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fps-from-a-headless-or-webgl-run-is-misleading)
- **Low or swinging fps** → another process is using the GPU; measure on an idle one. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fps-numbers-are-low-or-noisy)
- **A copied fps bench measures the wrong thing** → change its port, query string and polled phases. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#a-copied-fps-bench-measures-the-wrong-thing)
- **`ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX` in a Node script** → no constructor parameter properties or `enum` in code Node imports. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#parameter-properties-fail-in-a-node-script)
- **A new app's tests never run** → add its `vitest.config.ts` and register it in the root `projects` list. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#a-new-apps-tests-never-run)
- **`pnpm docs` does nothing** → it is a pnpm builtin; use `pnpm docs:gen`. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#pnpm-docs-does-nothing-useful)
- **`scene.schema.json` stale or in a merge conflict** → never hand-merge; regenerate it. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#sceneschemajson-is-stale)
- **`!important` vanished after a lint fix** → never run biome `--unsafe` over CSS. [Fix](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#biome---unsafe-removed-important)

## Before you invent a workaround

The demos in `apps/` hit most of these and solved them; [docs/examples.md](../../docs/examples.md) says which demo shows what, and the cookbook in [docs/cookbook/](../../docs/cookbook/README.md) has the patterns. If the fix needs an engine change, stop and tell the developer instead of editing `packages/` or `crates/`. Then prove the fix with [verify-your-work](../verify-your-work/SKILL.md).


===== skills/game-feel/SKILL.md =====

---
name: game-feel
description: Use when a Pebble3D game's core actions work but feel flat, at the game-feel step of make-a-game, or when a hit, jump, dash or win needs more impact. Layers hit-stop, shake, camera punch, trails, particles, decals, buffering, easing and sound, then tunes them by watching capture sequences.
---

# Game feel

A game whose mechanics work is a tech demo. A game where every press gets an answer you can see and hear, and the big moments land with weight, is a game. This skill is the polish half of the build: it comes after the core verbs work and before the art pass.

The values to start from, with the demo file that uses each one, are in [techniques.md](techniques.md). Ronin Outpost (`apps/katana-defense`) is the densest reference: read [present.ts](../../apps/katana-defense/src/game/present.ts), where every sim event becomes feedback.

## The process

1. **Pick the moments.** From the brief, choose the three to five moments that matter most: the hit, the jump, the kill, getting hurt, the win. Write them in `BRIEF.md` under a "feel" heading. Polish these deeply; everything else gets a basic cue.
2. **Give every action an answer.** Before layering, check that every input the player can make produces a visible change and a sound within a tick or two. Missing feedback is the most common reason a game feels broken.
3. **Layer each big moment.** Build the stack below, one layer at a time, capturing after each.
4. **Tune by watching** (the loop at the end). Feel lives in motion; a single frame cannot show it.

## The layers

Not every moment needs every layer. A heavy hit takes the full stack; a footstep takes a puff and a tick of sound.

| Layer             | What it does                                                           | Lives in     |
| ----------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------ |
| Hit-stop          | Freezes both sides for a few frames on contact, so the hit reads solid | sim          |
| Impact frame      | One to three frames of high-contrast flash on the heaviest hits        | presentation |
| Screen shake      | Trauma that decays; the offset is trauma squared                       | presentation |
| Camera punch      | The lens narrows by a few degrees and springs back                     | presentation |
| Slow motion       | Game time drops for the one decisive moment, then eases back           | presentation |
| Trails            | A tapering ribbon behind the striking edge or a fast body              | presentation |
| Particles         | Sparks, chunks and dust that arc with gravity and land                 | presentation |
| Persistent decals | Pools, cracks and rings that stay on the floor after the action        | presentation |
| Telegraphs        | Enemy wind-ups drawn on the ground before the hit                      | presentation |
| Input buffering   | A press slightly early still counts; cancel windows chain moves        | sim          |
| Easing            | Wind-up, strike, follow-through; exponential approach for cameras      | both         |
| Sound             | A cue per action and per hit, scaled by weight                         | presentation |

**A heavy hit reads best as a stack**, in this order on the timeline: the hit-stop freeze, an impact frame, screen shake starting as the freeze ends, a brief camera punch-in, a tapering trail on the striking limb that hangs during the freeze, particles that burst and arc with gravity, and decals that stay on the floor after the particles land. Each layer alone is subtle. Together they sell weight.

**Scale by weight.** Light, heavy and finisher hits should differ on every layer: Ronin Outpost's light cuts freeze for fewer frames, shake less and do not punch the camera at all. If everything is maximal, nothing is.

**Keep the sim deterministic.** Hit-stop and buffering change gameplay, so they are sim state driven by ticks. Everything else reads the sim's events after the tick and never writes back. No `Math.random` in either: spread particles with offsets from the loop index, and shake with sums of sines.

## Input feel

- Buffer presses for a few frames and let a press just after a move ends still chain ([combo.ts](../../apps/katana-defense/src/game/combat/combo.ts)). Presses during hit-stop are buffered too.
- Give moves cancel windows so the follow-up starts the moment the current move's commitment ends.
- For movement: allow a jump pressed just before landing and just after leaving a ledge. Never drop a tap shorter than one tick ([live-input.ts](../../apps/skyrun/src/game/live-input.ts)).
- Camera and character followers ease with `1 - Math.exp(-k * dt)`, never a fixed lerp per frame. Recipes: [custom-camera.md](../../docs/cookbook/custom-camera.md).

## Sound

Every action and every hit gets a WebAudio cue fired from the event queue after the tick, louder and lower for heavier events. Unlock the context on the first gesture, cap voices per frame, and keep sound off in fixed mode. The pattern and its gotchas: [audio-sfx.md](../../docs/cookbook/audio-sfx.md).

## Budget

Effects cost fill rate, and layered additive effects can cost several times more on the WebGL backend than on WebGPU. Pool every effect (one preallocated `InstancedMesh` per kind, oldest recycled), cap counts, and measure fps on both backends with the effects on screen, as [verify-your-work](../verify-your-work/SKILL.md) describes, before adding more.

## Tune by watching captures

Stills can look great while the motion is stiff. Judge feel in a sequence:

```bash
pnpm shot --app <name> --param demo=1 --ticks <just before the moment> --sequence 90:2 --scale 0.6 --no-frames --name feel-hit
```

`--sequence` writes an animated WebP of the moment (flags: [docs/verification.md](../../docs/verification.md); a real script with sequences: [capture-final.sh](../../apps/ringout/bench/capture-final.sh)). Find the tick of the moment by scouting it headless ([demo-bot-and-captures.md](../../docs/cookbook/demo-bot-and-captures.md)). Then loop:

1. Watch the sequence. For each chosen moment, name what is missing or too much: "the hit has no freeze", "the shake hides the target", "the sparks vanish in place".
2. Change one value, recapture the same tick with the same seed, and compare.
3. Stop when each moment reads at a glance in the sequence and a still from the middle of it still shows what happened (trail, particles in the air, a mark on the floor).

## Exit check

- Every player action has a visible and an audible answer.
- Each chosen moment has its layer stack, scaled by weight, and a `--sequence` capture that you watched shows it.
- Sim tests still pass and the determinism test still holds (feel code did not leak randomness or presentation state into the sim).
- The effects are pooled, and fps on both backends with the effects on screen is checked when you claim performance.

Next: [art-direction](../art-direction/SKILL.md).


===== skills/art-direction/SKILL.md =====

---
name: art-direction
description: Use when a Pebble3D game's look is still engine defaults, at the art-pass step of make-a-game, or when captures look flat, muddy or inconsistent. Commits to one look from the brief (palette, toon or PBR, lighting, post, composition) and judges captures against it over at least two improvement passes.
---

# Art direction

Default lighting on grey boxes reads as a tech demo, whatever the mechanics. A committed look, one palette, one lighting mood, one rendering style, carried through every object and the HUD, reads as a game. You do not need imported art for it: every demo below builds most of its world from primitives and code.

The scene fields for everything here are in [docs/scene-reference.md](../../docs/scene-reference.md); the post and toon recipe is [post-and-toon-style.md](../../docs/cookbook/post-and-toon-style.md).

## Commit to one look

Write the look in the "look" section of `apps/<name>/BRIEF.md` before touching the scene, in one short paragraph a stranger could check a screenshot against:

- **Mood and time of day.** "Dusk on a floating stone arena", "noon in a dusty quarry", "a dark keep lit only by lanterns".
- **Palette.** A background family, a ground family and one or two accent colours reserved for what the player must notice: the player, the threat, the goal, pickups. Write the hex values.
- **Style.** Toon or PBR (next section), and why it fits.
- **Reference.** One or two of the reference captures below that are closest in spirit, and what you take from each.

Every later choice is checked against this paragraph. If a choice does not serve it, drop it.

## Toon or PBR

| Choose | When                                                                                      | Demo                                                                                                                         |
| ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `toon` | Stylised characters, action, readability over realism; mixing primitives with glTF models | Ronin Outpost: [arena.json](../../apps/katana-defense/scenes/arena.json)                                                     |
| `pbr`  | Materials are the point (stone, metal, glass), physics debris, a moody lit interior       | Breakpoint: [site.json](../../apps/breakpoint/scenes/site.json); Ringout: [arena.json](../../apps/ringout/scenes/arena.json) |

`post.style: "toon"` bands the lighting, adds a rim and ink outlines. Objects your code builds need `ToonNodeMaterial` or `renderer.stylize`; the recipe has the details. Pick one and apply it everywhere: a toon character on a PBR ground with no outline reads as a mistake.

## Lighting and sky

- **Outdoor** (`environment.preset: "outdoor"`): an HDRI sky lights the scene; pick one that matches the time of day, and set the sun direction and colour to agree with it. Breakpoint pairs a clear noon sky with a warm sun.
- **Studio** (`"studio"`): a gradient backdrop from `horizon` to `zenith` and range fog of the same colour. Ringout uses a deep violet horizon, a navy zenith and a peach sun: a whole mood from three colours.
- **Dark interiors**: low ambient, and the light comes from things in the world (lanterns, emissive pickups), as in Lanternfall. Make sure the player and the threat are always lit.
- A low, warm, side-on sun gives long shadows and shape; a sun straight overhead flattens everything.
- Fog hides the ground's far edge and separates depth layers. Tint it to the sky.

## Post

- **Tone mapping and exposure.** `agx` (the default) is soft and natural; `aces` is punchier and more saturated. Raise exposure until the ground reads, not until whites clip.
- **Bloom** only on what should glow: emissives, beams, effects. Lower the threshold for a softer glow, never so low that sunlit ground blooms.
- **AO** grounds objects on the floor. Leave it on unless you measured it costing too much.
- Runtime changes (a dusk grade over waves, a photo exposure) go through `toneMappingExposure`, as the recipe shows.

## Composition and silhouettes

- **Readable at a glance.** In a capture shrunk to thumbnail size, you can still find the player, the threat and the goal. If not, fix value contrast first (light against dark), then colour.
- **Silhouettes.** Each kind of actor has a distinct shape: size, proportions, a hat or a weapon. Ringout gives every orb its own team colour and a name plate; Swarm Siege keeps towers pale and the swarm saturated.
- **Accent colour is information.** Reserve the brightest, most saturated colours for gameplay (the player, danger, pickups, the HUD's key number). Scenery stays quieter.
- **Camera framing.** The default view puts the action in the middle third with space in the direction of travel. Title and results screens can use a slow orbit with the subject off centre, leaving room for text, as Ronin Outpost and Ringout do.

## Stage dressing from primitives

An empty plane is the biggest tell of a tech demo. Dress the stage with what the brief's world would contain, built from boxes, cylinders and spheres with distinct materials: walls and crates, posts and rope, rocks, columns, distant silhouettes on the horizon. Vary scale and colour slightly per instance (seeded, never `Math.random` in the sim). Breakpoint's sites are hundreds of boxes; Skyrun's floating islands are simple shapes over a sea of cloud. Dressing should frame the play space, never hide the player.

## The HUD is part of the look

Use one type family, the palette's accent for the numbers that matter, a translucent panel colour taken from the scene, and consistent corner placement. The HUD must not cover the action. Compare the HUDs in the Ringout, Skyrun and Swarm Siege captures below.

## Reference captures

Committed looks from the demos (the site's 1280x720 WebP captures; how they are made: [site/README.md](../../site/README.md)):

| Look                                                  | Capture                                                                                                                                                              |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Toon outdoor, ink outlines, a blade trail             | [Ronin Outpost, light combo](../../site/public/shots/ronin-outpost/03-light-combo-slash.webp), [dusk wave](../../site/public/shots/ronin-outpost/08-dusk-wave8.webp) |
| PBR stone under noon sun, dust and debris             | [Breakpoint, impact](../../site/public/shots/breakpoint/03-impact.webp)                                                                                              |
| Studio dusk backdrop, team colours, bold HUD          | [Ringout, opening clash](../../site/public/shots/ringout/03-opening-clash.webp), [ring drop](../../site/public/shots/ringout/05-ring-drop.webp)                      |
| Dark interior lit by lanterns, a vision cone          | [Lanternfall, creep](../../site/public/shots/lanternfall/02-creep.webp)                                                                                              |
| Pastel sky, floating islands, soft fog                | [Skyrun, spire](../../site/public/shots/skyrun/14-spire.webp)                                                                                                        |
| Night, neon beams on a dark ground, a saturated swarm | [Swarm Siege, firefight](../../site/public/shots/swarm-siege/05-firefight.webp)                                                                                      |
| Racing, motion and speed                              | [Drift Drone](../../site/public/shots/drift-drone/09-photo-finish.webp), [Ghostline](../../site/public/shots/ghostline/08-ember-glamour.webp)                        |

Open them before you start and name, in the brief, what you take from one or two.

## Judge and improve

The art pass is at least two passes, each ending in captures you looked at.

1. Capture the moments from the brief (title, mid-play, the big moment, results) with the `?demo=1` bot, as [verify-your-work](../verify-your-work/SKILL.md) describes. Open every PNG the shot prints.
